Clinical appearance of a chronic violaceous/atrophic plaque with scattered indurated papules near a joint (shoulder) fits. Often associated with chronic inflammation (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis) or prior surgery/metal implants.

2) Intravascular (intravascular large B‑cell) lymphoma or other intravascular lymphoproliferative disorder — Considered because of dense nodular lymphoid infiltrate and lymphocytes within vessels producing violaceous plaques. Less likely than #1 because the report did not describe atypical large lymphoid cells, but this needs exclusion because it has systemic implications.

3) Reactive angioendotheliomatosis (retiform/reactive vascular proliferations) — Can present as violaceous plaques/purpura related to vascular/reactive endothelial proliferation in the dermis and can be associated with underlying systemic disease. Histology usually shows endothelial proliferation rather than histiocytic intralymphatic accumulation, so this is less likely.

4) Lymphatic malformation / lymphangioma circumscriptum with secondary inflammation — Clinically can produce clusters of papules/vesicles and violaceous appearance; histology would usually show dilated lymphatic channels, but chronic inflammation can alter appearance. Possible but less consistent with the prominent histiocytic intravascular component.

5) Kaposi sarcoma — Initially a reasonable clinical consideration for a chronic violaceous plaque, but HHV‑8 (LANA‑1) was negative and histology lacks spindle cell vascular proliferation, making this unlikely.
